chapters.title: Chapter 6: Putting Alternatives Into Your Portfolio

lessons.title: How Much in Alternatives? Sizing by Wealth, Liquidity Needs and Horizon

children.text: Most investing mistakes with alternatives are not about picking the wrong fund, flat or startup. They are about size. A good private credit fund becomes a disaster when it holds the money for your daughter's college fees. A sensible angel investment becomes reckless when it is half your savings. Five chapters have given you the tools to judge what an alternative really offers. This final chapter answers the practical question: how much, if anything, belongs in your portfolio? The answer comes from a sequence of gates and limits, not from how exciting the opportunity sounds.

body.text: Size alternatives from the outside in. First protect what you need, then work out what you can lock away, then cap how much any single bet can take. Only what survives all three steps is available for alternatives, however good the pitch.

children.text: Step 1: Pass the Gates First
Illiquid alternatives are for money that has no other job. Before any rupee goes into one, these gates should already be passed.

body.title: The five gates before any illiquid alternative
steps: An emergency fund of 6 to 12 months of expenses is sitting in a savings account, liquid fund or short FD
Adequate term life insurance and health insurance are in place for the family
High-interest debt such as credit card balances and personal loans has been cleared
Every goal due in the next 5 to 7 years, such as education, a home down payment or a wedding, is funded in liquid, lower-risk assets
A diversified core of listed equity and fixed income already exists, and you understand how it behaves in a crash

children.text: Step 2: Work Out What You Can Lock Away

markDefs.definition: The part of your investable wealth that no emergency, known goal or foreseeable need will require during an investment's lock-in period.

children.text: Chapter 2 introduced the liquidity budget. Here it becomes a calculation. Start with investable wealth: financial assets you could reallocate, excluding the home you live in. Subtract every rupee with a known job. What is left is your
lockable capital
. It is the ceiling for illiquid alternatives, not the target.

body.latex: \text{Lockable capital} = \text{Investable wealth} - \text{Emergency fund} - \text{Goals due before the lock-in ends} - \text{Buffer}
body.caption: Add a buffer of one to two years beyond any lock-in, because alternatives often run late

children.text: Apply the horizon test to every individual investment as well: its expected lock-in, plus a buffer, must end before the date you could possibly need that money. A 7-year fund is not suitable for money you might need in year 8 if funds in that category regularly extend by two years.
Step 3: Cap the Total and Every Single Bet
Even if a lot of capital is lockable, it rarely makes sense to lock it all. Two caps protect you from your own enthusiasm and from any one manager, platform or project going wrong.

body.caption: Illustrative ranges for illiquid alternatives by investable wealth (judgement-based guidance, not rules)
headers: Maximum in any single illiquid position

cells: Stick to listed options such as gold ETFs and REITs
Very small angel cheques; listed REITs and gold do not count as illiquid
SM REITs, small angel portfolios built slowly
AIFs become sensible from roughly ₹10 crore
Multiple AIFs across managers, strategies and years

body.caption: The wealth you need before a given minimum ticket fits within your single-position cap

body.title: When does an AIF fit?
body.prompt: An AIF requires a minimum commitment of ₹1 crore. If you never want a single illiquid position to exceed 10% of your investable wealth, what is the minimum investable wealth you should have, in crore?
body.explanation: ₹1 crore ÷ 10% = ₹10 crore. With a looser 20% cap, the answer would be ₹5 crore. This is why SEBI's ₹1 crore minimum makes AIFs a sensible fit mainly for investors with investable wealth well above ₹1 crore, not for those who just clear it.

body.text: Listed REITs and gold ETFs are alternative in what they own but can be sold the next trading day. They belong in your diversification plan, but they do not use up your lockable capital. Only count assets you cannot readily sell against the illiquid limits above.

children.text: Step 4: Count What You Already Own

Many Indian families are already deep into alternatives without calling them that. Studies of household finances, including RBI's 2017 Household Finance Committee report, found that the average Indian household held the large majority of its wealth in real estate and a significant share in gold, with only a small slice in financial assets. Before adding anything new, count:
Investment property and land.
A second flat or a plot is already a large illiquid alternative.
Your own business.
For owners, this is concentrated, illiquid private equity, and it is tied to your income too.
ESOPs and unlisted shares.
Startup-style risk, often in the same industry as your job.
Jewellery.
Part of your gold allocation, even if it is never sold.

body.text: If existing property, business equity or ESOPs already exceed your illiquid limit, the right amount of new private alternatives may be zero. Adding a PE fund to a portfolio dominated by a family business and two flats increases concentration; it does not diversify it.

children.text: Putting It Together: The Joshi Family

The Joshis in Ahmedabad have ₹3 crore of investable wealth, excluding the home they live in. They own no other property or business. Their son's college fees of about ₹60 lakh fall due in four years, and they plan a ₹40 lakh home upgrade in six years. They are 15 years from retirement.

body.caption: Sizing alternatives for the Joshi family (₹ lakh, illustrative)

cells: College fees ₹60 lakh, home upgrade ₹40 lakh
20% of ₹300 lakh, within the ₹1 to 5 crore range
Below both caps, to leave room for mistakes

children.text: Lockable capital is ₹188 lakh, but the total cap stops them at ₹60 lakh and the single-position cap at ₹15 lakh. A ₹1 crore AIF is ruled out, since it would be one-third of their wealth in a single bet. They choose ₹45 lakh: a ₹10 lakh SM REIT position, an angel portfolio of about ₹25 lakh built in small cheques across more than 10 companies over four years, and ₹10 lakh in a second income-oriented alternative. No single position exceeds ₹15 lakh.

children.text: Stress-Test the Size

markDefs.definition: When listed assets fall in value, illiquid assets reported at stale appraised values automatically become a larger share of the portfolio, even though nothing was bought.

children.text: A size that looks comfortable in normal times can become uncomfortable in a crash because of the
denominator effect
. Take a ₹5 crore portfolio: 50% listed equity, 30% debt and gold, 20% illiquid alternatives. Equity falls 35%, debt and gold gain 3%, and the alternatives report a 5% dip.

body.caption: A ₹5 crore portfolio before and after a crash (₹ crore, illustrative)

stats.label: If ₹40 lakh cash is then needed
stats.context: Withdrawn from liquid assets, the only ones that can be sold

stats.label: If alternatives truly fell 20%
stats.context: Real portfolio value, with alternatives at 20.2%

stats.label: Room to rebalance the alternatives
stats.context: They cannot be sold to restore the target

children.text: The stress test shows three things. Your illiquid share grows in a crash. Any cash you need must come from liquid assets, often at their lowest prices. And you cannot rebalance the illiquid part back down. Size alternatives so that the post-crash share is still acceptable, not just the starting share.

body.title: Pacing commitments to funds over time

markDefs.definition: The year a fund makes its first investments. Funds from different vintage years buy at different valuations, so spreading commitments across vintages reduces the risk of investing everything at a market peak.

children.text: Investors large enough for AIFs should rarely commit their whole alternatives budget in one year. Spreading commitments across three or four
vintage years

avoids buying everything at one valuation peak, as many investors who committed heavily in the 2021 startup boom learned. Because capital is called gradually and distributions come back over time, the amount actually invested is usually well below total commitments. Plan for the full commitment being called, though, since calls can arrive faster than expected.

body.title: The right order
body.question: Which sequence correctly sizes an allocation to illiquid alternatives?
options: Choose the most attractive fund, invest the minimum, then build an emergency fund from future savings
Pass the gates, calculate lockable capital, apply total and single-position caps, count existing illiquid assets, then stress-test
Invest the same percentage as a large family office, since they are experienced
Put all lockable capital into alternatives, because money not needed should earn the illiquidity premium
body.explanation: Sizing works from the outside in: protect what you need, find what can be locked away, cap it in total and per position, account for the illiquid assets you already own, and check the result survives a crash. Family office allocations assume far more wealth, stable liquidity and access.

body.title: Name the effect
body.textWithBlank: When listed assets fall and illiquid assets keep stale values, the illiquid share of a portfolio rises automatically. This is called the ___ effect.
body.explanation: The total portfolio value, the denominator, shrinks while the appraised alternatives barely move, so their percentage share rises. Institutions often find themselves over their alternatives limits after a crash for exactly this reason.

body.title: Mr Bhatia's three AIFs
body.scenario: Mr Bhatia, 52, owns a textile business in Ludhiana. His total wealth is about ₹8 crore: the business is worth about ₹3 crore, his factory land and two flats about ₹2.5 crore, and his liquid financial investments about ₹2.5 crore. His relationship manager suggests committing ₹1 crore each to three AIFs: a PE fund, a real estate credit fund and a VC fund, "because you have ₹8 crore, so 37.5% in alternatives is reasonable."
body.prompt: Apply this lesson's sizing steps and explain whether the recommendation makes sense.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Count what he already owns. The business (₹3 crore) is concentrated, illiquid private equity tied to his income. The land and flats (₹2.5 crore) are illiquid real estate. That is ₹5.5 crore, about 69% of his wealth, already in illiquid alternatives.

2. Use investable wealth, not total wealth. His liquid, reallocatable wealth is ₹2.5 crore. Three ₹1 crore commitments total ₹3 crore, more than all of his liquid investments. He could not even meet the capital calls without selling other assets or borrowing.

3. Single-position cap. Even one ₹1 crore AIF is 40% of his investable wealth, far above a 10% cap, which would require about ₹10 crore of investable wealth.

4. Correlation. His business, the real estate credit fund and his property all depend on the Indian economy and credit cycle. A downturn could hit his income, his business value and these funds together.

5. Liquidity. At 52, with business cash needs and retirement ahead, locking his entire liquid portfolio for 7 to 10 years leaves no buffer.

Conclusion: the recommendation does not make sense. His "37.5% in alternatives" is really closer to 100% once existing assets are counted. His liquid portfolio should stay mostly in listed equity, high-quality fixed income and gold, which diversify his business and property. If he wants exposure to listed real estate, REITs can provide it without further illiquidity.

points: Most alternative mistakes are sizing mistakes: good investments become bad ones when they hold money needed elsewhere or take too large a share.
Pass the gates first: emergency fund, insurance, no expensive debt, near-term goals funded, and a working liquid core.
Lockable capital is investable wealth minus emergencies, goals within the lock-in and a buffer; it is a ceiling, not a target.
Cap both the total and each single position: a ₹1 crore AIF at a 10% cap needs about ₹10 crore of investable wealth.
Count existing property, business equity, ESOPs and jewellery before adding new alternatives; for many Indian families the right new amount is zero.
Stress-test the size: in a crash, the illiquid share rises, cash must come from liquid assets, and the alternatives cannot be rebalanced.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Allocation ranges, caps and examples are illustrative guidance based on general principles, not rules or personalised recommendations. Your appropriate allocation depends on your full financial situation. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
